title: NRX reactor accident — Chalk River, Canada
incidentLocation: Chalk River Laboratories, Ontario, Canada
description: Partial meltdown of the NRX research reactor — the world's first major reactor accident. Operator error and mechanical failure caused fuel damage and significant radioactive release into the reactor core.

title: Kyshtym disaster — Mayak Production Association
incidentLocation: Mayak, Chelyabinsk Oblast, USSR
description: Cooling system failure at a nuclear fuel reprocessing plant caused a chemical explosion releasing 20 MCi of radioactivity — among the worst nuclear accidents ever. The Soviet government concealed it for 30 years; 22 villages were evacuated.

title: Windscale fire — Pile No. 1
incidentLocation: Windscale, Cumbria, England
description: Fire in the graphite core of a plutonium-production reactor — the UK's worst nuclear accident. Released radioactive contamination across the British countryside; milk from a 500 sq km area was destroyed for a month.

title: Broken Arrow: Mk-17 hydrogen bomb dropped near Albuquerque
incidentLocation: Kirtland AFB, Albuquerque, New Mexico
description: An unarmed Mk-17 ten-megaton hydrogen bomb was inadvertently jettisoned from a B-36 during landing approach to Kirtland AFB. The conventional explosives detonated on impact 4.5 miles south of the airfield; no nuclear yield, but a 25-foot crater.

title: Broken Arrow: Tybee Island bomb (still missing)
incidentLocation: Wassaw Sound, off Tybee Island, Georgia
description: After a midair collision with an F-86, a damaged B-47 jettisoned its Mk-15 hydrogen bomb in shallow water off the Georgia coast to allow safe landing. The bomb was never recovered despite multiple searches; it remains buried in silt as of today.

title: Broken Arrow: Mk-6 bomb dropped on Florence, SC
incidentLocation: Mars Bluff, near Florence, South Carolina
description: A B-47 accidentally released an unarmed Mk-6 nuclear bomb during a transatlantic flight. The conventional explosive trigger detonated on impact in a rural backyard, creating a 70-foot crater and injuring six members of the Gregg family. The nuclear core was not aboard.

title: SL-1 reactor explosion — three fatalities
incidentLocation: National Reactor Testing Station, Idaho Falls, Idaho
description: Prompt criticality accident at an experimental US Army reactor killed all three operators on duty — the only fatal nuclear reactor accident in US history. A control rod was withdrawn beyond safe limits, causing a steam explosion.

title: Broken Arrow: Goldsboro B-52 crash (one safety switch from detonation)
incidentLocation: Goldsboro, North Carolina
description: A B-52 broke up in flight, releasing two 4-megaton Mk-39 hydrogen bombs. On one bomb, 3 of 4 arming devices activated — a single low-voltage switch prevented a detonation 260× the yield of Hiroshima. The other bomb's uranium core was never recovered.

title: K-19 submarine reactor accident
incidentLocation: North Atlantic, off Norway
description: Cooling system failure on Soviet ballistic missile submarine K-19 caused a reactor crisis. Sailors entered the reactor compartment without protective gear to perform emergency repairs; all eight died of radiation within weeks. The story was suppressed for decades.

title: Broken Arrow: Palomares B-52/KC-135 collision
incidentLocation: Palomares, Almería, Spain
description: A US B-52 collided with a KC-135 tanker during midair refueling, releasing four Mk-28 hydrogen bombs over Spain. Two bombs' conventional explosives detonated, contaminating 250 acres with plutonium. A third landed intact; the fourth was lost at sea and recovered after 80 days.

title: Broken Arrow: Thule B-52 crash on the ice
incidentLocation: North Star Bay, Thule Air Base, Greenland
description: A B-52 on airborne alert crashed onto sea ice 7 miles from Thule AB after a cabin fire. All four hydrogen bombs ruptured, scattering plutonium and uranium across the ice. A 700-person cleanup recovered most contamination; one bomb's secondary stage was reportedly never found.

title: K-129 submarine sinking
incidentLocation: Pacific Ocean, ~1600 miles NW of Hawaii
description: Soviet diesel-electric submarine K-129 sank with three nuclear-armed ballistic missiles aboard, killing all 98 crew. The CIA later raised part of the wreck in Project Azorian (1974) using the Hughes Glomar Explorer in one of the largest covert intelligence operations of the Cold War.

title: Three Mile Island accident — Unit 2
incidentLocation: Three Mile Island, Dauphin County, Pennsylvania
description: Partial meltdown of TMI Unit 2 — the worst commercial nuclear accident in US history. A stuck pilot-operated relief valve caused coolant loss; operators misdiagnosed the cascading failure for hours. About half the reactor core melted, but containment held.

title: Broken Arrow: Damascus Titan II silo explosion
incidentLocation: Titan II Launch Complex 374-7, Damascus, Arkansas
description: A dropped wrench punctured a Titan II ICBM's fuel tank during routine maintenance. After eight hours of leakage, the missile exploded, killing one airman and injuring 21. The W-53 nuclear warhead (9 Mt — the largest in the US arsenal) was blown 200 yards but did not detonate.

title: Chernobyl disaster — Reactor No. 4
incidentLocation: Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant, Pripyat, Ukrainian SSR
description: Catastrophic core meltdown and steam explosion during a safety test of the RBMK-1000 reactor. Released ~400× the radioactive material of Hiroshima; the 30 km exclusion zone remains largely uninhabited. Officially 31 immediate deaths; estimated long-term cancer toll varies widely.

title: K-219 submarine fire
incidentLocation: Atlantic Ocean, 600 miles NE of Bermuda
description: A leak in a missile tube caused a fire and explosion on Soviet Yankee I-class submarine K-219, killing four crew. The boat sank three days later with 15 nuclear missiles and two reactors aboard, ~18,000 feet down.

title: Goiânia radiological accident
incidentLocation: Goiânia, Goiás, Brazil
description: Scrap metal scavengers cracked open an abandoned cesium-137 radiotherapy source from a defunct clinic. The glowing blue powder was distributed among family and friends; 4 died, 249 were contaminated, and 112,000 were monitored. The worst non-power-reactor radiological accident in history.

title: K-278 Komsomolets sinking
incidentLocation: Norwegian Sea, off Bear Island
description: Fire aboard the deep-diving Soviet attack submarine K-278 Komsomolets caused it to sink in 1,680 meters of water. 42 of 69 crew died, most from hypothermia. The wreck still contains a reactor and two nuclear-tipped torpedoes; slow corrosion is monitored by joint Russian-Norwegian teams.

title: Tokaimura criticality accident
incidentLocation: JCO fuel plant, Tōkai, Ibaraki, Japan
description: Workers manually mixing uranium fuel improperly poured a critical mass of solution into a precipitation tank. The resulting prompt criticality lasted 20 hours. Two workers died of severe radiation exposure; one is the most-documented case of high-dose radiation effects in medical history.

title: Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster
incidentLocation: Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, Ōkuma, Fukushima, Japan
description: Magnitude 9.0 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami disabled cooling for three reactors, causing meltdowns and hydrogen explosions. Released the second-largest fallout total after Chernobyl. ~150,000 evacuated; only one direct radiation-attributed death officially recorded.

title: Nyonoksa radiation accident — Burevestnik test
incidentLocation: Nyonoksa, Arkhangelsk Oblast, Russia
description: Explosion during recovery testing of what Western analysts believe was a nuclear-powered Burevestnik (SSC-X-9 Skyfall) cruise missile. Killed 5 nuclear scientists, briefly raised radiation levels in nearby Severodvinsk 16× background. Russia has not fully disclosed details.

title: Broken Arrow: Yuba City B-52 crash
incidentLocation: Near Yuba City, California
description: A B-52 lost cabin pressure and crashed during emergency descent. Two nuclear weapons aboard had their safety devices intact; no nuclear or conventional explosion. Crew ejected; one died.

title: USS Scorpion submarine sinking
incidentLocation: Atlantic Ocean, ~400 miles SW of the Azores
description: USS Scorpion (SSN-589) sank with all 99 crew aboard. The cause remains officially undetermined; theories include a torpedo malfunction. The wreck contains a nuclear reactor and two nuclear-armed torpedoes. The Navy monitors the site periodically.

title: Broken Arrow: Cumberland B-52 crash
incidentLocation: Big Savage Mountain, near Cumberland, Maryland
description: A B-52 carrying two nuclear weapons broke up in severe winter weather. Three crew died. Both weapons were recovered intact in the snow, with minimal contamination.
